But you must not suppose from this sample of his sermons that he ever flew into real rages with his congregation. Not at all — and that was his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrible things to his crew in a tone so strangely mixed of fun and fury, with the fury seeming so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such odd invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides, all the while he himself looked so easy and lazy, handled his steering-oar so loungingly, and yawned so broadly — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, worked like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sorts of humorists whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous as to put all their subordinates on guard when it comes to obeying them.

But almost everybody supposed that this particular care in preparation on Ahab's part could only be with a view to the final chase of Moby Dick, for he had already revealed his intention to hunt that mortal monster in person. items.new: There is another little item about gamming that must not be forgotten here. All professions have their own little peculiarities of detail; so has the whale fishery. In a pirate, man-of-war, or slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern sheets on a comfortable, sometimes cushioned seat there, and often steers himself with a pretty little milliner's tiller decorated with gay cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no seat astern, no sofa of that sort whatever, and no tiller at all. High times indeed, if whaling captains were wheeled about the water on casters like gouty old aldermen in patent chairs. And as for a tiller, the whale-boat never allows any such effeminacy; and therefore, since in gamming a complete boat's crew must leave the ship, and since the boat-steerer or harpooner is one of that number, that subordinate is the steersman on the occasion, and the captain, having no place to sit, is rowed off to his visit standing bolt upright like a pine tree. And you will often notice that, conscious of the eyes of the whole visible world resting on him from the sides of the two ships, this standing captain is keenly alive to the importance of keeping up his dignity by keeping on his legs. Nor is this any very easy matter; for behind him is the immense projecting steering oar, hitting him now and then in the small of his back, while the after-oar returns the favor by rapping his knees in front. He is thus completely wedged in front and behind, and can only spread himself sideways by settling down on his outstretched legs; but a sudden, violent pitch of the boat will often go far toward toppling him, because length of foundation is nothing without corresponding breadth. Simply make a spread angle of two poles, and you cannot stand them up. Then again, it would never do, in plain sight of the world's riveted eyes — it would never do, I say — for this straddling captain to be seen steadying himself the slightest bit by catching hold of anything with his hands; indeed, as a token of his entire, buoyant self-command, he generally carries his hands in his trouser pockets; but perhaps, as they are generally very large, heavy hands, he carries them there for ballast. Nevertheless there have been cases, well-authenticated ones too, where the captain has been known, for an uncommonly critical moment or two — in a sudden squall, say — to seize hold of the nearest oarsman's hair and hold on there like grim death.
